The prompt isn't the intelligence. You are. The prompt just structures your thinking so Claude can help you think clearer.

Why Most "Second Brain" Systems Fail

The typical second brain workflow looks like this:

Find something interesting

Save it somewhere

Tag it

Link it to related notes

Review it weekly

Forget about it anyway

The failure point is always Step 3-5. The maintenance. Nobody maintains their system past week two because the overhead of organizing knowledge is higher than the value of retrieving it.

The fix: Remove the human from the organizing step entirely. Let AI handle the taxonomy, the cross-referencing, the summarizing, and the gap-filling. Your only job is dumping raw information into a folder.

The Architecture (Takes 5 Minutes)

Create a folder anywhere on your computer. Inside it, create three subfolders:

 

raw/ is where everything goes. Meeting notes, article clips, competitor screenshots, client briefs, SOPs, strategy notes, podcast transcripts, email threads. Don't organize any of it. Don't rename files. Just dump.

wiki/ is Claude's territory. It reads raw/, identifies topics, creates organized articles, links them together, and maintains an index. You never touch this folder by hand.

outputs/ stores every answer Claude generates when you query the system. Briefings, comparisons, decision frameworks. Each output feeds back into future answers.

That's the whole thing. Three folders and an instruction file.

The Instruction File (CLAUDE.md)

This is what separates a smart system from a dumb one. The CLAUDE.md file tells the AI what your knowledge base is about, how to structure it, and what rules to follow.

 

Why this matters: Without this file, Claude improvises every single time. The output quality varies wildly. With it, every interaction follows your exact decision-making framework. You're essentially giving the AI a job description on day one.

 

Loading Your Knowledge Base (The 15-Minute Sprint)

Most people create the folders, stare at an empty system, and never come back. Here's how to get past that resistance.

Set a timer for 15 minutes. Dump everything you already have:

Meeting notes from the last 30 days (copy-paste from wherever they live)

Client documents (proposals, contracts, briefs)

Competitor research (screenshots, pricing pages, feature comparisons)

SOPs (even rough drafts or bullet points)

Strategy notes (investor updates, quarterly plans, revenue models)

Content research (articles you've saved, podcast notes, bookmarks)

Email threads that contain important decisions

Don't rename anything. Don't organize it. Don't make it "presentable." The whole point is that you're offloading the organization to AI.

I run 30+ source files in my own system. Clipped articles, analytics exports, partnership research, content frameworks, client transcripts. None organized by hand. All searchable through the wiki Claude maintains.

When it finishes, you'll have an organized wiki with:

This is the moment it stops being a filing system and starts being a thinking partner.

 

Using It Like a Real Strategist

Once the wiki has 10+ articles, start querying it like you'd query a brilliant advisor who has read everything you've ever written:

 

 

 

 

The compounding effect: Every answer Claude generates, save it back into the system. Each query makes the next answer better because it has more context. After 30 days of regular use, the system knows your business better than most employees would after 6 months.

 

The Monthly Audit (5 Minutes, Non-Negotiable)

Once a month, run this prompt:

 

This prevents knowledge drift. If Claude writes something slightly wrong early on and you don't catch it, every future answer builds on that mistake. The monthly audit is your quality control layer. Five minutes of prevention saves hours of compounding errors.

 

Why This Matters for Small Business Owners

A fractional Chief of Staff costs $5,000-15,000/month. A full-time one runs $150,000-250,000/year. This system costs $20/month (Claude Pro) plus $0 (local folders are free).

It won't replace a human strategist forever. But for a business doing $500,000-5M that isn't ready for that hire, this fills the gap. You get:

Instant recall of every client conversation

Every competitive insight cross-referenced

Every strategic decision documented and retrievable

Available 24/7 with zero ramp-up time

Gets smarter every single week you use it

The business owners who build this now will have a 6-12 month knowledge advantage over everyone who keeps their strategy in their head and their notes scattered across 14 apps.

Write your CLAUDE.md file (5 minutes)

This article takes you from zero to working voice agent in under an hour.

You don't need to be a developer. You don't need to code.

All you need is a strong system prompt and a tool called VoiceFlow. That's it.

Let's jump in.

(btw I built this live on the Build With AI podcast if you'd rather watch it in screen-share format)

 

The mental barrier most people have around voice agents

People hear "voice agent" and think: chatbot but worse. Janky. Robotic. Frustrating for customers.

But a voice agent is fundamentally different from a chatbot.

A voice agent listens, decides, and acts using defined rules. A good voice agent is capable of executing real workflows.

The stakes feel high because they are. When a customer calls, they expect a professional experience. Get it wrong and it reflects on your entire business.

So here's what stops people: they never start, because they're afraid of getting it wrong in production.

The solution is to build them right before you go live.

 

The 3 Control Levels framework

Before you build anything, understand autonomy levels.

In the Loop (Most Control): Human approves everything. AI gathers information, human decides and acts. Traditional customer service model.

On the Loop (Medium Control): AI decides within defined rules, human supervises outcomes. This is where most voice agents live. The AI makes decisions, but you're monitoring.

Fully Autonomous (Least Control): AI decides freely. Humans only react if damage occurs.

Which one should you use? Ask this: What's the impact of a bad decision?

For appointment booking? Medium control (on the loop). For emergency situations? High control (in the loop). For customer onboarding? On the loop.

The impact determines your autonomy level.

 

The Architecture

Everything lives in a single Google Doc with two sections:

Section 1: Agent Instructions (Who you are, how you behave)

Identity and Purpose: "You're a virtual scheduling assistant"

Role: "Help customers determine if they need service, then book appointments"

What you DO: Schedule appointments, send confirmations, handle same-day requests

What you DON'T do: Troubleshoot problems, diagnose issues, speculate about safety

Voice and Persona: "Friendly but brief. Conversational but professional."

Speech Characteristics: "Sound human. Be transparent that you're automated, but don't be awkward about it."

Section 2: Knowledge Base (What you know)

Service area and zip codes

Business hours and appointment availability

Emergency vs. non-emergency procedures

Common services offered

What triggers an escalation to a human

That's your system prompt. Copy it and adapt it for your business.

 

Setting it up in Voiceflow

Step 1: Paste your prompt into a new project.

VoiceFlow automatically generates:

Conversation flow

Branching logic

Information collection steps

Escalation handlers

You don't diagram this by hand. VoiceFlow builds it for you.

Step 2: Add your knowledge base.

Export your facts (hours, services, pricing, emergency procedures) as a text file or Google Doc.

Upload it. VoiceFlow indexes it.

Now when the agent answers questions, it pulls from your knowledge base, not from general knowledge. This prevents hallucinations and keeps answers accurate.

Step 3: Connect data collection to a spreadsheet.

When the agent collects information (name, phone, service needed), it automatically dumps that into a Google Sheet.

One click to connect. No code.

You can route to Calendly, your CRM, Make.com, or any tool VoiceFlow integrates with (there are dozens).

Step 4: Test by calling it.

VoiceFlow gives you a phone number. Call it. Have a full conversation.

The agent will:

Ask your emergency question first

Check if your zip code is in service area

Collect your information one question at a time

Confirm details

Schedule or escalate

All without you touching code.

 

Why this works (the Clarity Principle)

Most voice agent projects fail because people jump straight to "build" without thinking.

They skip the planning phase.

But the real magic is in the prompt.

A weak prompt = weak agent. You'll spend days tweaking.

A strong prompt = one-shot success. VoiceFlow builds clean conversation flows automatically.

The difference = hours of upfront thinking.

Ask yourself:

What's my greeting?

What's the emergency check?

What's my triage?

What information do I need?

What happens if I can't help?

How do I handle frustrated customers?

When do I escalate to a human?

Answer those questions first. Everything else follows.

 

Edge case management

Edge Case 1: Asking the same question twice

Customer: "What's your phone number?" Agent: "I don't understand. What's your phone number?" Customer: (repeats) Agent: "I still don't understand."

Result: Customer rage. Bad experience.

Fix: If they fail twice on the same question, escalate immediately. Don't make them repeat themselves.

Edge Case 2: The apologetic agent

Agent: "I'm sorry, I don't understand. I'm so sorry." Customer: I don't care about your apologies. Just help me.

Fix: Empathy without excessive apologizing. Acknowledge. Move forward. Don't take on their problems.

Edge Case 3: The agent that won't give up

Customer: "I need an electrician." Agent: "Are you experiencing an emergency?" Customer: Silence or non-answer. Agent: (tries to diagnose the problem instead of escalating)

Result: Agent steps outside its lane. Quality drops.

Fix: Be explicit in your prompt: "Do not troubleshoot. Your job is to collect information. If you can't get the info you need, escalate."

LLMs will try to "win" by solving the problem. Guardrails prevent that.

Edge Case 4: The terrible handoff

Agent: "I'm transferring you to a human." (Phone disconnects) (Customer has to explain everything again)

Result: Terrible experience after a smooth automation.

Fix: When transferring, hand off with context. The human gets a summary: "Name: Susan. Location: Clarendon Hills. Issue: Electrical problem. Already collected: phone number, service address."

 

ROI breakdown

Time:

Manual scheduling: 5-10 minutes per call

Voice agent: 2-3 minutes per call

20 calls/day = 2.5 hours saved daily

Cost:

Part-time scheduler: $25-35/hour

Voice agent: ~$0.50-1.00 per call

600 calls/month = $300-600 vs. $2,000-2,800 for human labor

Quality:

After-hours availability: Your agent works 24/7

Zero scheduling conflicts: No double-booking

Consistent experience: Same professional greeting every time

 

Build yours this week

Monday: Define your flow on paper. Answer the 7 questions above.

Tuesday: Write your prompt in a Google Doc. Ask Claude to refine it.

Wednesday: Create your knowledge base document (hours, services, emergency procedures).

Thursday: Log into VoiceFlow. Create project. Paste prompt. Add knowledge base.

Friday: Test by calling your agent. Iterate based on what breaks.

Following week: Go live.

Total investment: $20/month (VoiceFlow Pro). No code or expensive devs required.

This week I crossed 50,000 followers on X.

Hard to believe, because when I started posting about AI, I had 15k. Every one of them came from my old life: selling on Amazon.

Most of you know me as an AI guy. You probably know nothing about how I got here.

Here are a few things about my background that might help you, especially if you feel stuck right now.

-I graduated college in 2017 with two degrees, entrepreneurship and marketing. Both basically worthless

- My first job out of college was at IBM selling data storage. I was 22, making $70k a year, which felt like great money at the time

-It didn't take long to realize I hated corporate life and didn't want that to be my future

-I stuck around long enough to go through a year and a half of IBM's Global Sales School, widely considered one of the best sales training programs in the world. I got paid to learn how to sell

-Right after graduation I began a side hustle selling used books on Amazon. I fell in love with it

-in 2019 I quit IBM to sell on Amazon full time, even though I was barely making any money doing it

-I moved across the country and back in with my mom to chase it

-I did not have immediate success, I got down to my last $1,000 in savings and had to take a $15/hour job at my uncle's insurance agency to keep the lights on. Still building Amazon on the side (January 2020)

-COVID hit and accelerated ecom. By August 2020 I quit the insurance job and went back to Amazon full time, this time actually making money

-That year I did $990k in sales, the next year over 3M, the next year over 4M

-In January 2023 I started posting content online. There was a huge gap in the market. Almost nobody was teaching the sales and relationship side of selling on Amazon

-That summer I partnered with @cleartheshelf and @entreresource  to launch my first info product, the Wholesale Challenge

-I had never sold an info product. I was brand new to content and marketing

-The Challenge was a 7-day cohort-based live training. $300 on the front end, with a $1,000 upsell webinar on the back

-I had never run a webinar in my life. I closed 52% of the room and we collected $110k in pure profit in under 45 minutes

-That was the moment I finally understood the power of building an audience, marketing, a personal brand, and putting out a genuinely good product

-About a year later I launched a mastermind and coaching program called The Wholesale Network

-we grew it to over $350k in ARR in under a year and a half

-By the middle of 2025 I was completely burned out on Amazon after doing it for almost 9 years

-selling on Amazon taught me every fundamental of business and I wouldn't trade those years for anything, but I knew it was time to move on (I just had no idea what was next)

-I sold The Wholesale Network to a partner, liquidated my Amazon storefront, and set out to figure out what I actually wanted to do with my life

-started experimenting heavily with AI, started building no-code automations with tools like Zapier and Make

-in January of this year OpenClaw took off and I was in the right place at the right time. My business partner found it on day two, back when it was still called clawdbot

-We started experimenting immediately and got about two weeks ahead of everyone else

-When it went viral, we were positioned to create the best content on how to actually use it, because we were already using it in our own business

-My following doubled in two weeks just from sharing what we were doing

-Since then we've built a real business: AI assessments, AI concierge consulting, and our AI Operator Academy community, which now has over 50 members

-We're partnering with top-tier brands, growing on every channel, and have more opportunities than we know what to do with

-All of it traces back to one thing: investing in the Build With AI podcast, social media, personal branding, and partnerships

-A year ago I genuinely didn't know what I was going to do with my life. I was pretty depressed. My entire identity was wrapped up in being an Amazon seller, and once that wasn't my path anymore, I felt completely lost

I'm writing this to tell you something simple: if you don't know what's next, keep moving forward. Keep putting in the work. Keep talking to people. Keep building your brand.

The opportunities will show up. And when they do, you'll be in a position to capitalize.

This guy runs his entire marketing department out of folders and markdown files. 

No code or crazy automations. He calls it CMOHQ, it works with any AI (Claude, ChatGPT, Hermes, Codex), and he sells the whole thing as a zip file. 

He went 3 weeks without opening his laptop and the business kept running.

@IMJustinBrooke is back on the pod to walk us through the entire system. Here's what I learned:

1. The whole OS is folders and markdown files. He tried n8n, LangChain, and CrewAI. Too technical for a copywriter.

2. One HQ folder for who you are. One folder per brand with intelligence, departments, and metrics inside. Say "work in the FaithFunnels brand" and Claude switches context.

3. He built the finance folder from a YouTube transcript. It ingests ThriveCart, Kit, Google Ads, and Zeni exports and auto-generates max CPA, spend ceilings, and dashboards.

4. Build it in iCloud, not on a Mac Mini. It's just text files. Phone, laptop, office, same brain.

5. Nothing skips the pipeline. Pope mentions "digital sobriety," Claude writes the article, he approves, it publishes to Ghost via MCP with an ElevenLabs audio version.

6. Reporting is wired in through MCPs. Kit, Google Analytics, Microsoft Clarity. Clicks to leads to sales, plus a monthly P&L drop.

7. He uses Claude Cowork, not Claude Code. 90% of the features, and his work is mostly writing anyway.

8. Start with Jobs To Be Done. Every job becomes a folder. Every folder gets instructions.

9. Delivery is the product. The zip holds an ops manual and an installer.md that interviews the buyer and builds their system. Zero onboarding calls.

10. If they want to build it themselves, they're not your customer. Millionaires look at the system and say "can I just pay you?"

His 2 key takeaways:

1. Every agent needs three things: memory, instructions, and tools. Get those right and you can replicate any process in any business.

2. Stop doing sales calls on the fly. Run a slide deck, tweak one slide per call, and by call five it's dialed in and trainable. That's how you get out of sales.

5. Set the boundaries.

-What can the agent read?
-What can it change?
-What requires approval?
-What must it never do?
-When should it stop and escalate?

6. Run acceptance tests.

-Test the normal path.
-Test missing data.
-Test conflicting instructions.
-Test an out-of-scope request.
-Test a failed connection.
-Test an action that requires human approval.

7. Launch with a human in the loop.

Reliable work is the goal, not a 100% hands off system.

-Quote turnaround.
-Completion rate.
-Backlog.
-Human interventions.
-Errors.
-Recovered work.
-Customer experience.

Establish the baseline, then report what changed.

Business rules change.
Offers change.
People change.
Systems change.

The knowledge base and agent need an owner, monitoring, and regular review.

HOW TO BUILD THE KNOWLEDGE LAYER EVERY AI AGENT NEEDS

before agents can be truly effective they need a strong context layer to operate from.

A real company knowledge base has a few non-negotiables:

1. One fact has one home.

Pricing does not live in a proposal, a Slack thread, three spreadsheets, and the founder's memory.

There is one canonical source. Everything else points back to it.

2. Knowledge is organized by function.

-Company.
-Customers.
-Offers.
-Marketing.
-Sales.
-Operations.
-Market intelligence.
-Integrations.
-Finance.

The exact map will change by business, but the rule stays the same: an agent should know where to look before it starts guessing.

3. Every important fact has context.

-Where did it come from?
-Who owns it?
-How sensitive is it?
-When was it last reviewed?
-Is it current, experimental, or planned?

Without this, an agent can retrieve information but cannot judge whether it should trust it.

4. Private data has a protected tier.

Credentials, customer records, contracts, and other sensitive information do not belong in the same place as general operating knowledge.

The knowledge base can hold a safe pointer. The protected system holds the actual record.

5. Agents get boundaries, not unlimited access.

A sales agent can read company context and maintain sales knowledge.

It should not be able to rewrite finance policy because it found a conflicting note in a call transcript.

6. Raw information has to be distilled.

Calls, emails, CRM updates, and documents are inputs.

They do not become durable company memory until someone or something reviews them, places the fact in the right home, and resolves conflicts.

7. Maintenance is part of the product.

A knowledge base that is correct once and ignored for six months becomes a more convincing source of wrong answers.

It needs an owner, an intake process, validation, and a regular cleanup cadence.

This is why I would lead with the knowledge base before the agent.

Once the company has one governed source of truth, every future AI project gets easier:

-New agents start with context.
-Humans stop hunting for answers.
-Workflows share the same rules.
-The business is less dependent on one person's memory.

a company's organized, governed, current operating knowledge is a massive moat, one of the few that are left in the AI age.

HOW TO DESIGN A MANAGED AI AGENT A BUSINESS CAN ACTUALLY TRUST

STOP pitching "AI employees." No one knows what that means.

START selling one defined function instead.

Here's the operating model:

1. Give the agent one job.

-Speed to lead.
-Speed to quote.
-Lead qualification.
-Knowledge-base maintenance.
-Meeting preparation.

A narrow job is easier to explain, build, test, and improve.

2. Ground it in the same company knowledge as the team.

The agent needs the offer, customer, process, policies, history, and current priorities.

It shouldn't reconstruct the business from random emails every time it runs.

3. Separate knowledge from action.

The knowledge layer tells the agent what is true.

The action layer lets it use email, calendar, CRM, documents, or other tools.

Keeping those layers separate makes the system easier to govern and manage.

4. Define what it can read.

Full company context may be useful but that doesn't mean every agent should see every confidential record.

5. Define what it can change.

A marketing agent should be able to maintain marketing knowledge.

It should not be able to edit finance rules.

We have tested this with positive and negative checks: an agent can make an in-scope change and gets rejected when it tries to write outside its domain.

That is a far better proof point than saying it is "autonomous."

6. Define what requires approval.

-External messages.
-Calendar changes.
-Public content.
-Destructive actions.
-Financial actions.
-Customer commitments.

Drafting and recommending are different from deciding and publishing.

7. Build acceptance tests before. thedemo.

-Can it find the canonical source?
-Can it refuse stale or conflicting information?
-Can it stay inside its write boundary?
-Can it escalate uncertainty?
-Can it recover when a connection fails?

Installation is not acceptance.

8. Show the work every month.

-What did the agent handle?
-Where did it fail?
-What changed?
-What still needs a human?
-What is the next improvement?

Managed agents are not software you install and forget.

They are a defined function you operate, monitor, improve, and keep aligned with the business.

The winning offer is: "we manage a specific piece of work, on top of your company's knowledge, with clear boundaries and human control"

The final step is boring but important: assign a human owner. Someone has to review failures, approve boundary changes, and keep the underlying knowledge current. A managed agent without an accountable owner slowly turns into unmanaged risk..

This business model is hiding in plain sight.

In the next few minutes, I'll show you how one non-technical operator is installing AI "employees" inside small businesses and getting paid a monthly retainer to manage them, with zero coding background and almost no audience.

I recently interviewed Phil Goodwin, a product designer who's completed about 21 agent setups and turned them into recurring revenue in roughly a month of running the managed model. 

I've spent the last year selling AI services to small businesses, and this is one of the cleanest early playbooks I've seen.

In this article, I'm giving you the entire playbook for selling managed AI employees:

The offer structure (and why most people package agents backwards)

How to pick the first role that creates the "light-bulb moment"

The dead-simple fulfillment setup (one Telegram group)

The weekly value ledger that proves ROI to your client

The exact pricing evolution from $500 setups to $1,000/month retainers

The 12-step paid-pilot sequence to land your first client

Almost nobody is talking about the managed layer of this business. That's the entire opportunity.

Let's get into it.

Sell a Role, Not an Agent

The foundation of this entire model is a positioning shift. Without it, nothing else matters.

Most people build an agent, install it, hand the client a login, and hope the business owner figures out the rest.

Bad idea.

A small-business owner doesn't wake up wanting a VPS, an LLM, or another AI tool. They want someone (or something) to own work they're tired of doing.

So Phil positions the offer like hiring a digital employee. One clearly defined role, usually admin or executive-assistant work.

What the AI employee comes with:

A clear job description

Company knowledge and memory

Access to the specific tools the role requires

A dedicated computer or server environment

Approval gates for consequential actions

Monitoring and repairs

Ongoing workflow coaching for the owner

How it operates:

A client request or scheduled job triggers the work

The agent uses company knowledge and connected tools

A human approves sensitive actions when required

The agent completes the work

The operator monitors the system and improves the workflow

The agent is only one part of the offer. The actual product is the managed business result.

One Thing to Note Before We Continue

A working agent doesn't automatically create adoption.

Phil learned this the expensive way. His first offer was one-time infrastructure setup, and he climbed from $500 to $1,000, $1,500, and $2,000 per project. He'd configure everything, give the client 14 days of support, and move on.

Some clients stopped using what he built.

The technology worked. The clients didn't. They had no idea what to delegate, how to build workflows, or how to talk to an agent. They treated it like Google: ask a question, get an answer, leave.

That gap is exactly why the management layer exists, and it's a large part of what the client is actually paying for. You're selling adoption much more than you're selling the install.

Picking the First Role (+ a Real Client Example)

Don't promise a company unlimited agents. Most small businesses need one painful category of work taken off the owner's plate.

Good starting roles:

Central-office administration

Executive-assistant work

Research and prospecting

Recurring reports

File and document management

Content support

Here's what this looks like in the wild.

One of Phil's early managed clients runs a family directional-drilling business. The owner bounces between contractor hours, field logs, QuickBooks, PDFs, contracts, spreadsheets, and job folders all day.

In one request, the owner asked the agent to:

Search his inbox for an email from a specific person

Find an invoice for a particular job

Create a new job folder

Save the invoice PDF inside it

Extract the relevant info into a spreadsheet

Save the spreadsheet in Dropbox

Return the link

The agent came back with the completed sequence roughly 6 to 10 minutes later.

That's the light-bulb moment you're engineering. Not a flashy demo. A real piece of work the owner already understands and already hates doing.

Once that first workflow lands, the client starts asking the most important question in this entire business:

"What else can it do?"

The Fulfillment Setup (One Telegram Group)

Phil's smartest fulfillment decision costs nothing: he creates a Telegram group with three members. The client, the agent, and himself.

The client watches how Phil communicates with the agent. Phil watches what the client requests, spots unclear instructions, and identifies new workflows worth building.

It's observable coaching instead of forcing the client to learn alone.

The full management layer can include:

The shared client-agent-operator channel

A monthly workflow review

Monitoring and failure alerts

Repairs and maintenance

Human approval gates

A shared spreadsheet or other editable source of truth

Ongoing refinement of the agent's responsibilities

One rule Phil recommends: make the agent write important outputs into a human-readable system like Excel. Research shouldn't disappear into the agent's private memory. Payments shouldn't live only inside a chat. The client and the agent need a shared source of truth they can both inspect and update.

The Weekly Value Ledger (Proving ROI)

This was my biggest takeaway from the conversation.

Phil gives the agent a value ledger. Every task gets logged with what was completed, how long it would normally take a person, the estimated dollar value of that time, and which tasks still need a baseline from the client.

I'd expand it into a weekly report the agent sends the owner every Friday:

 

If the agent doesn't know how long a task normally takes, it asks.

That last part matters. The goal isn't to invent impressive ROI numbers. It's to make the estimate visible, let the client correct it, and improve the ledger over time.

Phil's drilling client's ledger estimated roughly 63 hours returned in the first week, and he separately described an estimated $6,300 week. Those are ledger estimates, not audited savings, which is exactly why you agree on the time baseline and hourly value with the client up front.

Most AI operators report what they built. Clients care about what the system did. A weekly value report turns an invisible retainer into a visible operating record.

Getting Your First Client (No Audience Required)

Phil had around 1,500 followers on X when he started. His early clients came from friends, local relationships, and referrals. Not a content funnel.

The sequence was simple. He built agents for himself first. Then he invited people he already knew to test the service with a fully transparent pitch: 

"I'm testing a managed-agent service. I'll install the agent, help you build workflows, and charge you a lower early-client price while I improve the offer."

That's a stronger position than pretending to be an established expert, because the client knows exactly what they're getting:

A lower early-adopter price

More attention from the operator

A chance to shape the service

Honest expectations about where the offer is today

In return, you get experience, feedback, proof, and potentially a referral. Phil's early friend projects introduced him to paying clients in completely different markets.

Pricing (Match Your Price to Your Proof)

Phil's pricing evolved with the maturity of the offer. Here's the full progression:

Early infrastructure-only setups: $500 to $2,000, one-time.

First managed pilots: No setup fee, roughly $250/month to cover infrastructure while he learned the model in two industries.

Recent managed engagement: Roughly $1,500 setup + $500/month, including a monthly call, the shared Telegram channel, and ongoing support.

Stated target: Roughly $2,000 setup + $1,000/month per agent. That's his target, not pricing he's proven repeatedly yet.

The lesson isn't to copy his numbers. It's to match your price to the proof you currently have:

Don't absorb the infrastructure and model costs yourself

Charge for at least some of your time

Explain why an early client is getting a lower price

Document the work and results

Raise prices as fulfillment gets repeatable and value gets provable

You don't need to start at $5,000/month. You also don't need to work for free. You can get paid to learn, as long as the client knows that's exactly what's happening.

Optimizing the System & Pro Tips

1. Run the 12-step paid-pilot sequence

If I were starting from zero:

Build an agent for yourself first

Pick one deployment environment and learn it well

Find one business owner in your existing network

Identify one painful, repeatable role

Sell a transparent paid pilot

Define the agent's permissions and approval gates

Create a shared client-agent-operator channel

Write important outputs into a shared source of truth

Track every task in a weekly value ledger

Validate the estimates with the client

Turn the first clear win into a testimonial or referral

Raise pricing only when proof and fulfillment improve

2. Expand the role, not the headcount

Don't rush to sell agent number two. Deepen the first role until the client is asking for more.

3. Respect the risk

If an agent can access email, financial files, company records, or client data, you're responsible for permissions, security, approval boundaries, monitoring, and recovery. Non-technical doesn't mean unaccountable. Stay inside what you can fulfill safely and bring in technical help when the risk exceeds your competence.

Final Thoughts

The agent build gets you through the door. The management, coaching, reliability, and proof are what make the service worth renewing.

You don't need to know everything before you start, you just need to be one useful step ahead of the client, honest about where you are, and capable of staying with the system after launch.

Stop using AI to collect business ideas. That's a waste of time. Instead, use Codex to do everything that comes after the idea: offer, pricing, pitch, website, and a walk-in prospect list, all in under 25 minutes. 

Below is the full breakdown: every decision, every deliverable, and the exact playbook I used to turn an experiment into a real business.

 

This is the foundational work that most folks tend to avoid in the early stages of a new venture:

What exactly are you selling?

Who are you selling it to?

What should you charge?

How will you fulfill it?

What will you say when you walk through the door?

Which businesses should you contact first?

So I opened voice mode inside Codex and gave it a simple assignment:

Help a completely non-technical operator build an AI services business from scratch.

Less than 25 minutes later, I had:

A defined local AI service

A simple offer and pricing model

A one-line sales pitch

A recommended fulfillment stack

A privately published website

A Google Sheet with 10 nearby prospects

A route ordered from closest to farthest from my neighborhood

I didn't make money in 25 minutes.

I hadn't sold the offer, installed the system, or proven the pricing would work.

But I'd removed most of the blank-page work between "I want to sell AI services" and "I can walk into a business tomorrow with something specific to pitch."

That's the opportunity.

Here's the entire process:

The five service ideas Codex proposed

Why I combined lead recovery with review growth

The exact offer, pitch, and proposed pricing

The simple tech stack behind it

How Codex built the website

How it found the first 10 prospects

The playbook I'd use to turn this experiment into a real business

Let's get into it.

Start with a painful problem that sits close to revenue

I didn't ask Codex for the most futuristic AI business possible.

I asked for something a non-technical person could start, sell to local businesses, and scale if it worked.

Codex proposed five services:

Appointment recovery

Review growth

A local content engine

Estimate follow-up

A simple front-desk chat assistant

The first two stood out because the value is easy for a business owner to understand.

Missed calls and ignored web inquiries become lost appointments.

Completed jobs without review requests become lost reputation and future demand.

Both problems already exist inside the business. Instead of trying to convince the owner they need some abstract AI transformation, we're simply showing them where leads are leaking and where good customer experiences are disappearing without producing public proof.

That's a much easier sales conversation.

The lesson: if you're choosing your first AI service, start with a painful workflow that sits close to revenue.

Bundle two outcomes into one clear offer

Instead of selling appointment recovery and review growth as separate services, I asked Codex to combine them.

The result: a "Local Lead and Reputation Engine."

The promise:

We help local businesses turn missed calls and new inquiries into booked appointments, then automatically turn happy customers into five-star reviews without adding work for their team.

The proposed offer included:

Instant text-back for missed calls

Immediate follow-up for website and social inquiries

A simple booking or callback flow

Appointment reminders

Automated review requests after a completed job

A monthly scorecard showing activity and results

Done-for-you setup and ongoing management

Codex also proposed a seven-day setup promise: setup fee refunded if the system isn't ready on time.

That's a guarantee around something the operator can actually control: implementation speed.

This matters because most weak AI offers describe the technology.

They sell automations, chatbots, workflows, and integrations.

The business owner doesn't care.

They care about answering more leads, booking more appointments, and earning more five-star reviews.

Sell the business result. Keep the AI in the fulfillment layer.

Make the pitch simple enough to say at the front desk

Once the offer was clear, I asked Codex to turn it into something I could say out loud while walking into a local business.

The one-line version:

We help local businesses turn missed calls and new inquiries into booked appointments, then automatically turn happy customers into five-star reviews without adding work for your team.

Then the three-step explanation:

We install missed-call text-back and instant follow-up so every lead gets a fast response.

We connect a simple booking flow and reminders so more people actually schedule.

After each job, we automate review requests to grow the business's Google rating.

That's enough for an initial conversation.

You don't need to explain models, agents, APIs, or workflow logic at the front desk.

The owner needs to understand the leak, the outcome, and how little extra work their team will have.

If your offer takes five minutes to explain, it's still too complicated.

Run the technology behind the scenes

My biggest concern was fulfillment friction.

I didn't want to sell a service that required the client to learn several new tools or replace systems they already use.

Codex recommended one platform, such as GoHighLevel, as the back-end layer.

The operator configures:

Missed-call text-back

A shared inbox for new leads

Follow-up messages

A booking-link connection

Review requests tied to the client's Google profile

The client keeps doing two things:

Respond to hot leads

Mark jobs or visits complete

Everything else runs behind the scenes.

If a prospect already has a sophisticated CRM and strong processes, integrate lightly or skip that client at the beginning.

The easiest first clients are businesses with no meaningful CRM, or businesses that barely use the one they have.

Your positioning becomes:

We don't replace your current systems. We add a managed response and review layer around them.

That's a much lower-friction offer than asking a small-business owner to rebuild how the entire company operates.

Price the pilot before you have proof

Codex proposed a simple founding-client structure:

$750 one-time setup

$500 per month

Cancel anytime after 90 days

After the operator has real proof and repeatable fulfillment, the suggested range increases to:

$1,500 to $2,500 for setup

$750 to $1,250 per month

These were proposed prices, not prices I charged or validated during the experiment.

That distinction matters.

The point wasn't that $500 per month is the perfect price for every niche.

The point was to start with a model that's easy to explain, covers the technology and management work, and gives the operator enough time to create a result.

I wouldn't start with pay-per-lead pricing.

It adds attribution fights before you have proof, data, or a reliable baseline.

A setup fee plus a predictable monthly retainer is easier for both sides to understand.

Once you know what a recovered appointment is worth, how many leads the system touches, and how reliably it performs, you can improve the pricing from evidence instead of guessing.

Build the minimum sales asset

Once we had the idea, offer, pitch, pricing, and stack, I asked Codex to build a website using Codex Sites.

It named the business Signal Local and created a simple site around one promise:

Turn every local lead into momentum.

The page explained the service in plain language:

Respond to missed calls and new inquiries quickly

Follow up until a lead books or speaks with the team

Ask satisfied customers for Google reviews

Set everything up without forcing a new workflow on the staff

It also included a working consultation button, a three-step explanation of the system, and a clear list of everything in the offer.

The site was published privately during the experiment.

Was it perfect?

No.

It was roughly 90 percent there. I still wanted to adjust a few visual details and tighten some copy.

But that's the point.

The website didn't need to win a design award. It needed to make the business look credible enough for the next sales conversation.

Don't spend three weeks polishing a brand before you know whether anyone wants the offer.

Build the minimum sales asset, then go talk to the market.

Find prospects based on visible business leaks

The last step was turning the offer into a prospect list.

I asked Codex to find 10 independently operated service businesses near my neighborhood in Charlotte with:

Strong Google reviews

A weak or missing website presence

Signs of being owner-operated

A physical location I could visit

I also asked it to put the businesses in a Google Sheet and order them into a practical route.

Codex used public signals only.

It explicitly noted that a missing website link isn't proof a business lacks a CRM. It's a prospecting signal, not a fact.

Two examples from the list made the opportunity obvious.

King Auto Repair showed a 4.5-star rating with 251 reviews and no website link displayed on Google Maps at the time of the research.

Plaza Tire and Auto showed a 4.7-star rating with 140 reviews and no website link displayed there either.

Both appeared to have real customer demand and established reputations. But neither offered an obvious online path to request a quote or book an appointment.

Their recent review activity suggested another opportunity: help the business consistently ask satisfied customers for reviews and professionally respond when negative reviews appear.

Codex added mobile-friendly Google Maps links to the sheet so I could open each profile while visiting the businesses.

That turned generic lead research into an actual walk-in list.

The strongest prospecting insight wasn't "find businesses that need AI."

It was this:

Find businesses with visible demand, then identify where their current process is leaking money.

The playbook I'd use from here

At the end of the experiment, I had enough to begin selling.

Not enough to claim the business worked.

Enough to run the first real test.

If I were taking Signal Local from experiment to operating business, here's the sequence:

Pick one niche with frequent inbound calls and valuable appointments.

Speak with five owners before making the offer more complicated.

Confirm how missed calls, web inquiries, booking, and reviews work today.

Sell one transparent founding-client pilot.

Collect the setup fee before building the full system.

Install only the workflows required for that client's process.

Track response time, conversations, bookings, review requests, and reviews generated.

Send the client a simple monthly scorecard.

Document every setup step as a reusable checklist.

Turn the first verified result into proof, then raise the price.

The most important step is number two.

Codex can generate the idea, package the offer, build the website, and organize the prospect list.

It can't replace the conversation with the business owner.

That conversation tells you whether the problem is painful, whether your proposed workflow fits reality, and whether anyone will pay.

Final thoughts

AI didn't build me a proven business in 25 minutes, but it did something more useful than generating another list of ideas.

It compressed the work required to reach the first real sales conversation.

I went from a blank page to:

One defined problem

One productized offer

One proposed pricing model

Ten local prospects

That's enough to stop researching and start testing.

They'll be the ones who use AI to move faster, then do the human work AI can't do for them:

Walk through the door.

Close the first client.

Deliver the result.

Turn that result into a repeatable business.

Week 1: Pick the job. Write down what information comes in, what access the agent needs, and how long the work takes a person today.

Week 2: Build two tasks the client repeats often. Run them in shadow mode, which means using real work without letting the agent send messages or make changes on its own.

Week 3: Put the client, the agent, and the person managing it (you) in one shared channel. Watch every request and save important results somewhere everyone can read.

Week 4: Fix what failed, check the weekly scorecard with the client, and decide whether another task is worth adding.

What work was completed?
How much human checking was still needed?
What broke?
What value did the client confirm?

Stage 1: Run a free mini AI assessment

The free mini assessment is a 15-minute conversation with a business owner.

Your job is to find one painful bottleneck and prescribe one practical fix.

Ask questions like:

Where does work tend to pile up?

Which manual task keeps stealing time from you or your team?

What have you tried to automate before that didn't work?

If one process got easier this month, which one would matter most?

You'll probably uncover several problems. Rank the top three, then focus on the best opportunity.

The prescription can be an off-the-shelf AI tool or one AI workflow the owner could build. If the owner spends five hours a week sorting email, you might recommend SaneBox as a simple starting point. The recommendation is the deliverable.

Don't install it for free.

That boundary matters. You're giving the owner a useful plan, not donating an implementation project.

After the first call, schedule a five- to 10-minute follow-up. Walk through the three opportunities you found, explain the one you'd fix first, and give the owner a simple next step.

Then make two asks:

Ask for a testimonial or referral if the assessment was useful.

Offer a paid assessment to find three to seven more opportunities.

Only run this free version for your first one to three prospects. Its job is to build confidence, collect proof, and create a natural transition into paid work.

Stage 2: Sell the deeper diagnosis

The paid AI tools assessment uses the same basic process, but goes much deeper.

Instead of a 15-minute interview, spend 45 to 60 minutes mapping the owner's most important workflows. Instead of prescribing one fix, identify three to seven AI opportunities.

Score each opportunity on two dimensions:

Impact: How much money, time, or capacity could this improve?

Effort: How hard will it be to implement and maintain?

Start with the high-impact, low-effort opportunities. In most cases, those are existing AI tools the business can adopt without a custom build.

The assessment should also document the assumptions behind the ROI.

Ask the owner how much each bottleneck costs in time every week. Then ask what an hour of their time is worth.

Say a business owner spends five hours a week in email and values their time at $250 an hour. That makes email a $1,250 weekly time cost. If a tool cuts the task from five hours to one, the estimated time value returned is $1,000 a week.

That's an estimate, not audited savings. The important part is that the owner supplied both inputs. You're not making up a dramatic ROI number after the call.

Package the findings in a professional report that includes:

The workflows discussed

The top bottlenecks

Three to seven recommended tools or workflows

An effort-versus-impact ranking

The assumptions behind each ROI estimate

A prioritized action plan

(you can download the exact template I use for my reports for free at audittemplate.ai)

Then schedule a 30-minute follow-up to present it. Walk through each problem, your recommended fix, and why it earned its place on the roadmap.

I started pricing these assessments at $500. I later sold them for $1,000, which was high enough for clients to take the work seriously and still easy for qualified owners to approve. I currently sell them for as much as $2,000.

No testimonials yet? Start at $1,000. That's what worked for me. Raise the price as your proof and delivery improve.

The assessment makes money on its own, but its bigger job is exposing the work that belongs in a recurring AI concierge engagement.

Stage 3: Turn the roadmap into a monthly retainer

AI concierge is done-with-you consulting for owners who know they need AI but don't know how to apply it to their business.

My standard engagement includes:

Two 45-minute strategy calls each month

Ongoing voice-message access through Voxer

One scoped workflow improvement at a time

Help building reusable Claude Skills inside Claude Cowork

Documentation and team training for the new process

The work follows a framework I call AOA: audit, optimize, automate.

Audit the process

Ask the client to share their screen and show you how the work gets done today. Capture each step without trying to fix it on the spot.

If customer onboarding takes 30 minutes, watch the full sequence. Note where information comes from, which tools the employee opens, what decisions they make, and where the process slows down.

Optimize it before adding AI

Most manual processes contain unnecessary steps.

If the current onboarding workflow has 14 steps and only needs 11, remove the waste first. Automating a bloated process only makes the bad version run faster.

Automate the cleaner version

Once the workflow is clear, turn the optimized process into a Claude Skill. During the call, guide the client through the build, the prompts, and the setup.

This is done with the client, not handed over as a black box. Adoption goes up because the owner understands what the skill does and how it fits into the business.

After the skill works, use Claude to help document the new SOP and train the rest of the team.

Then move to the next workflow.

The list rarely gets shorter for long. Clients cross off one problem, then notice two more opportunities because they finally understand what AI can do inside their operation. That gives the engagement room to continue as long as the work keeps producing value.

Three ways this model breaks

The offer is simple, but it's easy to ruin the economics.

1. You turn the free assessment into free implementation

One bottleneck. One prescription. Stop at the roadmap.

If you build the workflow during the free engagement, you remove the reason to buy the paid next step and teach the client that your implementation time has no value.

2. Two calls quietly become unlimited calls

My cadence is two 45-minute calls each month. I respond to Voxer messages within 12 business hours, but I don't add unscheduled Zoom calls for free.

Set that expectation before the engagement begins. If a client wants more calls, charge for the added access.

3. You build a different technology stack for every client

Trying to master Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, Zapier, and a pile of niche tools at the same time will crush your margin.

I standardize the core fulfillment process around Claude Cowork and Claude Skills. The skills can be adapted if the preferred AI platform changes, but I don't relearn the entire delivery stack for every account.

Standardization is what turns consulting into a business you can repeat.

You don't need to become an engineer. You need to ask good questions, recommend useful tools, improve a process before automating it, and keep the client moving.

before you tell a client their AI agent is ready, try to break it.

Use this checklist:

1. Does it have one clear job?
Write down what starts the job and what measurable result it should produce.

2. Does it know what information to trust?
List the approved sources, which one wins if two disagree, and what the agent must ignore.

3. Can it actually use its tools?
Test every action it needs: reading, creating, updating, attaching, and sending.

"Connected" doesn't mean the action works.

4. Does it have only the access it needs?
Sending a customer message, spending money, or deleting data should require human approval.

5. Does it know what to do when something goes wrong?
Test missing information, conflicting information, duplicate records, broken tools, and unclear requests.

6. Has it practiced on real work without taking live action?
Give it real inputs, but don't let it send customer messages or make changes you can't undo. Compare its decisions with a person's.

7. Have you tested the normal path, every known failure, and the same input twice?

8. Are you recording the job, result, proof, human review time, errors, and value?

9. If it breaks, who gets alerted and how do they undo the change?

An agent is ready when the client knows what it can do, where it stops, and what happens when real life gets messy.

we recently mapped a 25-step onboarding process for a client before asking AI to automate any of it.

It touched chat, project management, community access, email, payments, and shipping physical items.

For every step, we asked:

What starts it?
What could send it down a different path?
What does the system do?
Who is still responsible for the result?
How do we know it's finished?
What happens when something unusual comes up?

Once the map was done, AI proposed 5 repeatable skills and estimated that, once built and unblocked, they could automate 19 of the remaining 24 steps.

The map also showed why a certain step (a specific payment setup) wouldn't work for every client:

Standard payment options were easy to automate.

Unusual payment terms still needed a person to create the right product and checkout page.

The blueprint's rule was simple:

Automate the standard path. Send unusual payment terms to a human.

If we would've tried to automate the entire process from the start it would've been a disaster.

I: Why leads die in your inbox

Here's the uncomfortable math of running a service business: the lead you answer in 10 minutes closes, and the lead you answer in 2 days ghosts.

I know this because I sell AI assessments and retainers, and my pipeline lives in Gmail. Warm yeses come in while I'm on client calls, recording podcasts, or at the gym. By the time I see them, the buying energy has cooled.

I tried the standard fixes. A follow-up label system I stopped maintaining after a week. Todoist reminders that told me a lead existed but did nothing about it.

The problem was never knowing I should follow up. The problem was that following up required me.

So when Grok Bot launched, I didn't build a research assistant or a content bot first. I built the thing that touches money: a Revenue Closer whose only job is turning warm yeses and live pipeline into booked calls and paid deals.

 

II: What Grok Bot actually is (60-second version)

Quick context if you missed the launch. On August 11th, xAI released Grok Bot in early beta: always-on AI agents that each get their own computer in the cloud. Per xAI's announcement, they sign into the tools you already use, work across apps and inboxes, and only come back to you when something needs approval.

A normal AI chat stops when you close the window. A Grok Bot keeps running on its own machine, on a schedule, whether your laptop is open or not.

Two practical notes before you copy my setup:

Access. Grok Bot isn't sold standalone. It comes with SuperGrok, SuperGrok Plus, and SuperGrok Heavy plans, plus Cursor Pro, Pro+, Ultra, and Cursor Teams plans, with its own separate usage allowance. If you're already on one of those plans, this bot costs you nothing extra to try. If you're not, factor the subscription into your math before you build.

Connections. The Revenue Closer needs Gmail, Google Calendar, Todoist, and Google Docs connected. It works your real pipeline, so it needs your real tools.

My bot paid for its subscription multiple times over in its first day.

III: The Role, Skills, Routines stack

Here's the framework behind every bot I build now, and the reason this one worked on day one. I call it the Role, Skills, Routines stack:

Role: one system prompt that defines what the bot owns, what it sells, and what it's forbidden to do

Skills: reusable procedures the bot runs the same way every time

Routines: scheduled tasks that fire those skills without you asking

Most people write a vague "you are my sales assistant" prompt and wonder why the bot freelances. The Role layer is where you prevent that. Here's mine, templatized so you can drop in your own business:

REVENUE CLOSER SYSTEM PROMPT

 

A few of those lines are scar tissue worth explaining:

"Reply to their last inbound, never your last outbound." Gmail will bounce the To: field back to you if the bot replies to your own message. I learned that one the annoying way.

"Never invent a pay link." An AI that fabricates a Stripe URL in a money thread is a liability. The bot reuses links only if they already appeared in the thread or are the current public signup URL.

"Stay quiet when there is nothing new." A bot that pings you hourly with "no updates" trains you to ignore it. Silence is a feature.

 

IV: The three skills

Skills are where the bot stops being a chatbot and starts being an employee. Each one is a fixed procedure with a fixed stopping point.

Note: The skill prompts below are abbreviated to keep this article from being 3,000+ words. The full skill prompts, system prompt, and 3 routine prompts can be found in the Revenue Bot Playbook (free).

SKILL 1: DRAFT MONEY FOLLOW-UP

 

SKILL 2: DRAFT QUIET LEAD FOLLOW-UP

 

SKILL 3: PREP MONEY CALL

 

Notice the pattern across all three: every skill ends in a draft or a doc, never a send. And every skill has explicit skip conditions, because knowing when NOT to act is most of what makes an assistant trustworthy.

V: The three routines

Routines are what make this a closer instead of a tool you have to remember to use. Mine run on three schedules:

ROUTINE SCHEDULES

 

 

 

 

The hourly sweep is the one that made me $999. A warm lead landing at 2:14pm gets a drafted response by 3pm at the latest, not whenever I next open my inbox.

The division of labor matters too. The sweep owns fresh opportunities. The nudge routine owns silence. Neither touches the other's lane, so you never get duplicate drafts on the same thread.

VI: The $999 close, play by play

Here's exactly what happened in the first 24 hours.

An inbound lead hit my inbox asking about my $999 AI assessment. I was heads-down on other work and didn't see it.

The hourly sweep caught it. The bot read the thread, recognized it matched offer #1 on the ladder, and ran the Draft Money Follow-up skill. It pulled voice samples from my recent sent mail, wrote a reply in my voice with one clear ask, and pinged me: who, what they wanted, draft sitting in Gmail unsent.

I read the draft, made zero edits, and told it to send.

The prospect replied with a question. The bot drafted reply number two, this time including the Stripe link for the assessment, since the fee was already named in-thread. I approved. It sent.

He paid immediately.

 

Total human time on my side: maybe 4 minutes across two approvals.

Now the honest framing, because this is where most AI content lies to you:

The bot didn't generate this lead. My content and referrals did. A Revenue Closer multiplies inbound. It doesn't create it.

The win was speed, not persuasion. The draft was good, but the reason he paid is that he got a sharp, personal response while he was still in buying mode.

That last point is the entire thesis. You need your existing pipeline worked within the hour, every hour.

VII: Guardrails, and who should build this

Quick recap of the full system before you build:

One Role prompt that defines the offers, the voice, and the hard rules. Three Skills that always end in a draft or a doc. Three Routines that fire them on a schedule and stay silent when there's nothing to say.

Two guardrails I won't compromise on, and you shouldn't either:

The draft-only rule. The bot never sends without my explicit approval. Ever. It's tempting to remove the approval gate once the drafts get good. Don't. One hallucinated price or wrong-recipient email in a money thread costs you more trust than the gate costs you in seconds.

Access honesty. This bot reads my real inbox and calendar. If you're not comfortable being accountable for what an agent can touch, scope its access down or don't build it yet. Non-technical doesn't mean unaccountable.

And who this is actually for:

Build this if you're a service business owner with real inbound flow: leads from content, referrals, or past clients that currently sit in your inbox for hours or days.

Skip this if you have no inbound yet. A closer bot with an empty pipeline closes nothing. Go do the outreach and content work first, then come back. Also skip it if you'd need a new $200+ subscription just to access Grok Bot and you're not already getting value from those plans. The math should work before the bot does.

Only after a clean week, let it run without daily babysitting. Keep the approval gate forever.

The Revenue Closer works because it's narrow. It doesn't do content, ops, or admin. It does one job: make sure no warm dollar dies of neglect in my inbox.

If they won't pay $97 to learn from you, they were never paying $5,000 a month.

 

Rung 1: The $97 workshop

Dino built a three-hour virtual workshop on AI basics for orthodontists. One email to his list of roughly 5,000. No ads.

21 people in the room. 15 paid (he comped 6 existing clients). Some caught a $49 early-bird rate, the rest paid $97.

Three hours of teaching the Three Outcomes filter, applied to their industry. That's it. He's a trainer by trade, so this rung plays to his strength. But the content itself came from what we teach, customized to his niche.

Two things make this rung work:

The niche can afford you. Dino quotes Alex Hormozi on this: solve rich people problems. Orthodontists run practices doing seven figures. A $997 assessment isn't a purchasing decision for them, it's a rounding error. Pick a niche where your eventual retainer price is normal, not shocking.

The upsell starts before the workshop. The moment someone registers, the confirmation page offers the assessment: normally $997, but $497 if you grab it right now. Four people bought before the workshop even happened. He was up over $2,000 before delivering a single minute of content.

 

Rung 2: The assessment (and the deliverable that sells the retainer)

At the end of the workshop, Dino pitches the assessment again: $997, or $797 if you buy within 24 hours. Three people closed on the spot. Two more came in days later at full price.

That's a 44% close rate from the workshop room.

The assessment itself follows the process we teach: a deep discovery call, transcript into Claude, and out comes a scored report mapping AI solutions to their specific pain points against the Three Outcomes. You don't need to know how to build anything to deliver this. You need to ask good questions and let the AI do the analysis.

But Dino added one thing that I'm now stealing for my own business.

The 7-minute explainer video. He runs the finished assessment through Notebook LM (now Gemini's video tool) and generates a short animated video that walks the client through their own report. Their pain points, in their words, played back to them with the plan to fix each one.

Here's the prompt structure he adds to his assessment build:

EXPLAINER VIDEO PROMPT

Take this completed AI assessment report and write a prompt for Notebook LM that will generate a ~7 minute explainer video.

The video must:

- Address the client by name in the opening line

- Lead with the single biggest outcome (e.g. "designed to give you 5+ doctor-hours back every week")

- Replay the client's own stated pain points in their own words

- Walk through the plan as: "First we'll do X. Second, Y. Third, Z."

- End with the projected annual savings figure from the report

Why this matters for landing the retainer: your buyer is almost never the only decision-maker. There's a spouse, a partner, a business manager, a financial coach. One of Dino's prospects promised her financial coach she wouldn't buy anything without running it past him first. Instead of hoping she could re-explain a 20-page report, she forwards a 7-minute video.

The video does your selling in rooms you'll never be in.

He also has Claude prep his sales call from the same assessment:

SALES PREP PROMPT

From this assessment report and discovery call transcript, give me:

1. The client's 3 biggest pain points, ranked by emotional weight

2. Their stated financial goals and any hard numbers attached

3. Which sections of the report to slow down on during the walkthrough call, and which to move through quickly

4. A suggested call flow that connects our plan to their #1 goal

Real example: one client wants to sell her practice in five years for at least $1.2 million. Claude flagged that her EBITDA needs to hit roughly $500-600K to get there. So Dino's entire walkthrough connected every recommendation to that exit number. She's expected to sign this week. That's a target, not a closed deal yet, and I'm labeling it as one.

Rung 3: The two-path close

After the assessment walkthrough, the retainer pitch is one sentence. Here's the structure, pulled straight from how Dino (and I) run it:

TWO-PATH CLOSE SCRIPT

"I promised you a blueprint, and this is it. You now have everything you need to go save $[X] a year.

You've got two options. You can take this blueprint and implement it yourself, or hand it to any AI person you trust. It's yours.

Or you can hire us to do it for you. I've got the people and the process in place. You sit back and collect the results.

Which one sounds better to you?"

No pressure. No countdown timers. The genuine willingness to let them walk is what closes the deal, because it proves the assessment wasn't a trojan horse.

And think about who's hearing this. An orthodontist with patients, staff, and a practice to run. Implementing the blueprint themselves means 200 hours they don't have. Paying $30,000 to capture $250,000 in projected annual savings is the easiest math they'll do all year. (That $250K is the assessment's estimate, not audited savings, so say so on your calls too. Honest numbers close better than inflated ones.)

One sales psychology note from Dino worth bolding: he never says "$30,000." It's $5,000 a month. The only time the full number comes up is in the ROI comparison: pay 30 to get 250 back.

 

The math behind $65,734

From one $97 workshop, before marketing beyond a single newsletter email:

Workshop revenue: ~$1,500 (15 paid seats, mix of $49 early bird and $97)

Assessment revenue: ~$4,200 (4 pre-workshop at $497, 3 at $797, 2 at $997)

Cash collected before delivering a single assessment: $5,734

First retainer closed: $30,000 ($5,000/month, 6 months)

Second retainer: expected this week (target, not proven)

Behind that: 3 more assessment clients in the pipeline

Total value from one workshop: $65,734. The closed, verifiable portion is the $5,734 collected plus the $30K contract signed. The rest is pipeline, and Dino presents it that way too.

Notice the structure of the funnel math: the workshop and assessments aren't really the money. They're paid trust-building. The retainer is 84% of the total value. But you can't skip to it. The retainer only closes at that price because the client has bought from you twice, watched you deliver twice, and seen their own numbers in your report.

 

Getting your first client: who this works for

This model works if you have at least one of these:

A niche you already serve or understand (Dino: 15 years in orthodontics)

An email list, even a small one (his took 10 years to build to 5,000, but 21 registrants means you'd get similar results from a list of a few hundred in a tight niche)

A willingness to run a warm-network version: 5-10 personal invites to business owners you know, same ladder, smaller room

Who this isn't for: if you want to skip the assessment and go straight to building agents for strangers, this playbook won't save you. The ladder is the product. And if your niche can't afford $997 for an assessment, fix the niche before you fix the offer.

One more thing Dino said that should remove your last excuse: not knowing the industry deeply can actually be an advantage. His discovery calls run 90 minutes because his expertise pulls him into rabbit holes. The core assessment questions, the basic ones we hand you, produce the report either way.

You don't need to be the expert. You need to be the person holding the filter.

The first 10 actions I'd take from zero

Pick one niche where owners clear $500K+ and already pay for consulting.

Customize the assessment question bank to that niche (feed Claude what you know about their world and have it adapt the questions).

Build a 3-hour workshop teaching the Three Outcomes filter applied to that niche. Charge $97.

Set up the registration flow with the assessment upsell on the confirmation page: $997 anchored, $497 pre-workshop price.

Fill the room with one email to your list, or 20 personal invitations if you don't have a list.

Deliver the workshop. Close the assessment at the end with a 24-hour $200 discount.

Do 1-2 free assessments for existing contacts first to collect testimonials before the paid ones land.

Run every paid assessment through the discovery-call → Claude → scored report process.

Generate the 7-minute explainer video and send it as the teaser before the walkthrough call.

On the walkthrough call, run the two-path close. Quote monthly, not total. Anchor against their projected savings.

Then do it again next month. Dino's second workshop already has 10 paid seats, zero comps.

Final thoughts

The reason most people never land their first AI retainer is that they ask for marriage on the first date. Dino got paid to build trust three separate times before the retainer conversation ever happened, and by then it wasn't a pitch. It was the obvious next step.

He's 53, can't code, and plans to ride this until the wheels fall off.

Your excuses are gone.

The positioning shift: the workshop is not the product

Here's the line from Mark that reframed the whole model for me:

"I don't think the in-person workshop is the full value. It's getting your foot in the door. It's a lead magnet that you happen to make some money off of."

Most people who hear "AI workshop" picture the workshop as the business. Book them, deliver them, repeat. You can make a living that way. Mark's estimate is that you cap out at a couple hundred thousand a year, because workshops eat hours. Planning, delivery, and by his own account, he's wiped for days afterward.

So he uses the room differently. A workshop gets him in front of a whole team for 4-8 hours, with permission to ask about every process they hate. By the end, he has a list of expensive problems, a warm relationship, and the right to propose the build.

I'm calling this the Workshop Wedge: a paid, in-person session that opens the account, surfaces the real problem, and sets up a larger implementation deal. Four rungs.

 

Rung 1: the free artifact

Mark gives away as much as he can up front. A Claude skill, a bundle of assets, a short audit. Something the prospect can use today.

The point is trust before money. If you're targeting a company, this is what gets the workshop conversation started. If you're running a public workshop, this is your content on LinkedIn or X that makes someone click the Eventbrite link.

Sometimes there's a half step here: a paid audit. If he's going into a team, he'll diagnose their problems first and then tailor the workshop to what he found. That audit is also where the assessment in "workshop plus assessment" comes from.

Rung 2: the paid workshop

Two flavors, two price points.

Public, per head. His first was $495 a person, four hours, 15 attendees. Rough math: around $7,400 for an afternoon, before venue costs. The audience skewed 45 and older, people who were afraid of being left behind at work and didn't want to ask in front of their team.

Private, per company. Half a day to two days, $15K to $25K. Formats he's run: a team AI essentials session, a hackathon where he teaches the basics and then the group spends four or five hours building with Claude Code and Cowork together, and a "everyone leaves with an agent built" session.

I asked him directly about pricing because I'm in the middle of this myself. Two days before we recorded, my realtor here in Charlotte asked me to run a paid workshop for her brokerage. Every realtor is an independent contractor, so nobody's boss foots the bill. My gut said $500 a head.

Mark's answer: right in range, and don't go higher than you have to.

"You can make mistakes at $500. You probably can't make mistakes at $2,000 a head."

His logic is that a $500 attendee leaves saying "that was a bargain" and refers three friends. A $2,000 attendee scrutinizes every minute. For a first workshop, you want the referral, not the margin.

Rung 3: the custom build

This is where Mark says the money and the fun are.

$25K to $50K, three to six weeks. And he's clear that's the low end. He's been pulled toward mid-market and enterprise, with several six-figure proposals out right now. Those are bundles: assessment, workshop, training, build, and sometimes a short retainer, on one contract.

What he builds: what he calls an AI operating system. A context layer that connects three to five of their existing tools and their internal knowledge base into one place. His last startup did this for sales teams. Now he builds custom versions.

The receipt he gave: a client had one brilliant person spending seven hours a day on internal staffing, bouncing across eight platforms. Work got batched, spilled into weekends, quality slipped.
