Seven hours to 15 minutes is the sales pitch for rung three. The workshop is where he found it.

 

How the workshop finds the build

Mark writes something down every time this happens: in the middle of a session, someone on the team nudges the person next to them and says "we could do this for our quoting process." Three other people say "I was thinking the same thing."

That's the first build. I'm calling it the elbow test. If a process makes people elbow each other, it's expensive enough to pay for.

 

Rung 4: the next system and the retainer

After the first build, it branches.

Sometimes it's another workshop for a different team: engineering, customer success, a security and governance session for leadership. Sometimes it's the next build. Sometimes it's a retainer, and Mark's experience is roughly 50/50 between clients who want him for another three months and clients who want one big package, paid half up front and half on completion.

He doesn't chase maintenance fees. His view: if he's collecting maintenance, he failed at training the trainer. He'd rather parachute in, ship, hand off, and leave. So the retainer, when it exists, is for building the next thing, not babysitting the last one.

The math behind the ladder

Here's why the ladder matters more than any single rung.

Public workshop: $500 x 15 people = $7,500 for a day. Do one a month and it's $90K a year, and that's your ceiling if every seat fills.

Private workshop: $15K to $25K for one to two days. Ten of those is $150K to $250K. Still a ceiling, and you're cooked for a week after each one.

Build: $25K to $50K over three to six weeks. One build a month at the low end is $300K a year, and each one came from a workshop you already got paid for.

So the sequence, using Mark's low-end numbers: $7,500 public workshop, which produces one private workshop at $15K, which produces one build at $25K. That's $47,500 from one Eventbrite listing. The public workshop is 16% of that revenue.

He turns down workshops that don't have upsell potential, and he's said he could run far more if he weren't doing the bigger builds. But the shape holds: the workshop is the smallest check in the chain and the one that opens up the rest.

 

Getting your first workshop

Mark's advice for someone who's never run one: don't overthink it.

Three steps.

Pick a niche you already know. Mark's biggest regret is being too broad. Every one of his seven offers could be its own business, and now he has to choose. If you spent ten years in real estate, dental, roofing, or e-commerce, run "AI for [that]." 

I have an Amazon wholesale background. I could charge $1,000 to $2,000 a head to Amazon sellers and deliver more than I could to realtors, because I know what their week looks like.

Run one public, paid, in person. Eventbrite listing, Stripe up front, $500 a head. DM everyone you know in the area and ask who else should be there. If two people show up, you made money and they got the best workshop of their life. Worst case, you're out a couple hundred bucks on a room.

Don't teach everything. Mark's point that I keep coming back to: we live in a bubble. Most people's entire AI experience is typing into ChatGPT. They don't need 27 agents. They need Cowork or ChatGPT set up, two or three skills built, a couple of scheduled tasks, and a clear answer to "what's eating hours of your week that you hate?" That's the 80/20.

 

Then the upsell. Mark guarantees that if you do a great job, people will come up afterward and ask if you can do this for their company. Say yes.

 

Be upfront about what you haven't done. Trade a discount for a case study. That's how you go from one public workshop to your first private one without an audience.

Who this is for, and who it isn't

This is for you if you can build, or you're confident you can learn to build what you'd teach. You have a niche or an industry you know cold. You're comfortable in a room. Bonus points if you have an events or events-marketing background, because filling seats is half the job.

This isn't for you if you want fully remote, zero-travel work. It's not for you if you'd rather sell a $5K workshop and disappear; the model only pays off if you deliver well enough to earn the upsell. And it's not for you if you can't say "I've never done that, but I'm confident I can" with a straight face.

Three ways this model breaks

1. Selling workshops to teams that don't need you. Mark turned down a company that was already good at AI. They negotiated hard on price and he could see no upsell behind the workshop. If a team has real internal builders, you're a one-time line item. Qualify for "one person is the AI expert and everyone else is behind."

2. Overdelivering on complexity. Teaching a room of 50-year-old business owners about agent loops and orchestration is how you lose them in the first hour. The value is in simple, real jobs to be done. Tools are almost irrelevant. Workflows are the whole thing.

3. Treating the workshop as the finish line. If you walk out with a check and no opportunity log, you ran a class, not a wedge. The 48-hour proposal after the session is where the money is. Skip it and you've capped yourself at a couple hundred grand a year with the hardest possible schedule.

Pick the industry or persona you know best. One. Not "small business."

Write down the three workflows in that niche that waste the most hours per week.

Build a free artifact that solves one of them (a Claude skill, a prompt pack, a checklist). Post it.

Take the case-study discount on the first private one if it gets you in.

After the private workshop, propose the build. $25K to $50K, three to six weeks.

Turn down the next workshop that has no upsell behind it.

Final thoughts

Mark raised $8 million to build a product. The thing that out-earned it was standing in a room showing people how to use Claude.

His numbers are his, from six months of part-time experiments, and he'd be the first to say he's still figuring out which rung to double down on. But the shape is what matters: the free thing earns the room, the room earns the problem, the problem earns the build.

I'm making $8,000 a month building Claude skills for other people's businesses.

Every engagement runs on one framework I call AOA: Audit, Optimize, Automate. 

Here's the entire model:

1) Most people skip straight to Automate. That's the fun part. It's also how you end up automating a broken process.

2) Audit first. The client shares their screen and walks the process in painful detail while I take notes in a Google Doc and interrupt with a million questions.

3) Capture the plumbing, not just the steps. Who owns each step, which tool it runs in, where the data lives, and whether that tool can connect to Claude.

4) Hand the audit doc to Claude and ask it to find a better way. Then push back. Claude's first synopsis is usually partly wrong, and the client catches it.

5) Cut the fat. Most processes are 15 steps and only need to be 11. Most clients use 3 tools where 2 would do.

6) One home per fact. One client stored customer data in ClickUp and the CRM. We killed the ClickUp copy. Duplicates are just human error waiting to happen.

7) Have Claude write the build plan. It splits the process into skills, scaffolds each one, and lists next steps. Then you lock the doc.

8) A skill is a markdown file plus reference files. A reference file is just an example of what good looks like. Claude builds all of it.

9) Build one skill at a time from the build plan. If the audit was done right, Claude one shots it. Test on a real run, let Claude interview you, iterate. Version 2 is usually the keeper.

10) Draft first, never auto send. A speed to lead skill drafts replies for review on day one. It earns auto send later.

Two things that make this work:

1) Audit and Optimize are 80% of the work. Automate is the 20%. You have to earn the right to build.

2) Skills do one thing well. Split at every point a human or a wait interrupts the chain, then let an orchestrator run them back to back.

Useful way to test an AI agent before delivering it to a client (6 tests):

1. Source test. List the approved sources, which one wins when two disagree, and what it must ignore.

2. Tool test. Run every action it needs: read, create, update, attach, send. "Connected" doesn't mean the action works.

3. Access test. Make sure sending a customer message, spending money, or deleting data requires a human approval step.

4. Mess test. Feed it missing info, conflicting info, duplicate records, a broken tool, and an unclear request.

5. Shadow test. Real inputs, zero live actions. Compare its decisions to a person's before it goes live.

6. Repeat test. Same input twice. Same answer twice.

Then write down who gets alerted when it breaks and how they undo the change.

Installation is not acceptance. An agent is ready when the client knows what it can do, where it stops, and what happens when real life gets messy.

Never automate a workflow on day one. Run it through 3 stages:

Stage 1: You run it by hand
Take one process, run it yourself (manually), review the required steps and the output. Do this a few times.

Stage 2: Someone else runs it
Your assistant runs the same manual process and sends you the result to approve. You're now checking outputs, not making them.

Stage 3: An agent runs it
The agent runs the process and drops the output in an approve/reject queue. You only see the queue.

The biggest mistake people make is jumping straight to stage 3 then trying to debug an automated process that was never optimized in the first place.

How I get AI + my human assistant to do 50% of my work each day before I get out of bed:

I use Todoist to track my daily to-dos. Each task inside Todoist gets a description that follows a simple formula:

Why, Done, Access, Who

Why = the purpose of the task
Done = what does done look like
Access = what tools are needed to complete the task
Who = who is responsible for completion

Every morning Codex looks at Todoist at all the tasks due that day.

For any tasks where "Who" = Codex, it just completes the task.

This could be drafting follow ups, writing an email broadcast, scheduling a UPS pickup, or any number of other things.

For any task where "Who" = me or my assistant, Codex drafts a brief in the comments section of the task. The brief is designed to do as much of the task as Codex possibly can so that we can step in and finish it off.

The brief may add additional context, an exact phone number to call, a specific person I personally need to reach out to and the details of our last interaction, etc.

I highly recommend following the Why, Done, Access, Who context model for task management.

It's kinda a pain to add all those details for simple tasks like "book haircut" but 30 seconds of additional effort on your part enables your AI (or your human) assistant to take entire tasks off your plate in one shot.

@RyanLockAI runs one of the hottest startups in this space (Polyshares) and walked me through his entire business model on the pod.

Here's what I learned:

1. Making an intro to a data buyer is only step one. Technical due diligence on how the business actually operates is where the value gets built.

2. Labs buy the full workflow. Client email to internal Slack debate to resolution, including the fixes the team rejected.

3. He targets companies with 50+ employees, 3+ years on the same software, US-based, English. Below 50 employees = fixed legal and diligence costs kill the deal.

4. Remote-first white collar wins. If the work happens on the phone, the lab just sees "ticket created, ticket closed."

5. Depth of history beats raw volume. 20 years in business means nothing if they switched software 3 years ago.

6. Never let sellers de-identify their own data. Names become "employee 632" so relationships survive. DIY versions wreck the value.

7. Use a third party to de-identify. They hold the raw files for about a week, then delete them. That kills the biggest objection.

8. Never sign a perpetual license. 24 months of exclusivity is the typical buyer ask.

9. Time the exclusivity to the exit. Selling in 2 years? Match the term so the new owner inherits a dataset they can license again.

10. Demand rotates. A few weeks ago labs wanted heavy construction. Now it's video game companies.

His 2 key takeaways:

1. Act like a sell-side broker, not a lead seller. Organize and present the owner's data like an M&A deal and you can earn an advisory fee on top of the finder's fee.

2. The buyer pool could explode. If enterprises start training their own models, buyers go from maybe 10 labs to hundreds of thousands.

The fix takes 90 seconds.

Add a set of custom instructions (full prompt below) that tell it:

2. If anything I say conflicts with the brain, flag it and quote both versions

A generalized version of my prompt is below (works whether your brain lives in GitHub, Obsidian, Notion, etc.):

-------

These apply to every task in every project. A project's own instructions file (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, a project README) can add rules, but the conflict rule and the response rules below always apply.

## Context: my second brains

My second brains hold the context you need about me and my business. Use them as context for every task.

| Brain | Where it lives | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Company brain name] | [GitHub repo / Notion workspace / Obsidian vault / Drive folder] | [Company name]: team, offers, pricing, customers, brand, marketing, sales, operations |
| [Personal brain name] | [Where it lives] | Me: profile, preferences, schedule, goals, relationships, personal brand |

How to use them:

1. Read them directly through your [GitHub / Notion / Google Drive] connector. Always read the current version. Do not rely on cached copies or what you read in an earlier session.
2. If the connector is unavailable or cannot reach a brain, tell me in one line before starting the task. Never guess at what the brains say.
3. Read each brain's rules file first ([AGENTS.md / README / "Start here" page]). It holds that brain's routing map and rules.
4. Before each task, read the notes that bear on it. When unsure which brain owns a topic, check both.
5. Keep brain content private. Never move business facts into the personal brain or personal facts into the company brain.

## Conflicts: flag and ask

If anything I say, or anything we are working on, conflicts with either brain:

1. Flag it before acting on it. Quote the brain's version with its location, and the conflicting version with its source.
2. Ask me which is right and how the brain should be updated.
3. Do not edit either brain until I answer. Then propose the exact edit (location, current text, new text) and make it only after I approve, following that brain's rules file. For GitHub, open a pull request I can merge.

## How to respond

[Edit this section to your own style.]

- Keep responses concise. Answer first, no preamble, short paragraphs.
- Give one clear recommendation, not a list of options.
- Never use em dashes anywhere: replies, files, comments, commit messages. Use a comma, colon, period, or parentheses instead.

Phase 2: Feed it real inputs

I build every system the same way: Audit, Optimize, Automate (AOA). For a PR bot, that means getting the inputs right before anything runs on a schedule.

Have the bot run these in order:

/pr-strategist. Audience, positioning, news pegs. Mine landed on one play: be the practical source on AI agents for small businesses, built on "fix the process before you automate it." Cost: $1.05.

/voice-extractor. I fed it 20 LinkedIn posts I wrote by hand (3,616 words). It fingerprints sentence length, word choice, and punctuation, then enforces that voice on every draft. Cost: $1.50.

/newsjack-monitor-setup. Topics, competitors, feeds. Mine has 22 search terms and 3 feeds.

A proof-points file. Only claims I'll defend publicly, each with a source.

20 target outlets across 3 tiers, reporter names left blank until a story needs one.

Save profile.json flat. Top-level keys only, never wrapped inside a "profile" key. The detector ignores a wrapped profile without warning. In testing, the same content wrapped produced 0 search queries. Flat, it produced 18 queries and 113 scored signals.

The most important file is brief.md, specifically the "We never pitch" section:

 

Put it in the brief, not just your bot's instructions. In a test run, the detector flagged a Reuters story about AI agents used for hacking as pitch-ready. With the rule in brief.md, every run since has rejected it as a safety risk.

Short keywords collide, too. "Make" matched a SpaceX story. "Make.com" fixed it.

Last input: an expertise profile for /reactive-comment, so it knows which journalist requests you can credibly answer.

 

Phase 3: Schedule the routines

Now the Automate step. Set these four as recurring routines on your Grok Bot:

 

The morning slot gets drafts ready before noon, when editors read most. The midday sweep exists because request deadlines are often hours away. Every 90 days, the bot refreshes my voice fingerprint.

Skip Newsjack's own scheduler. The bot's routines handle timing, so there's one schedule to manage, not two.

A pitch pack is six skills in a row: /headline-generator, a 51 to 150 word pitch in my voice, /fact-check, /meanest-editor, /find-journalists, and /same-outlet-ranker to pick one reporter per outlet.

Phase 4: The Three-Gate Rule

Every draft has to clear The Three-Gate Rule before it reaches me:

The Editor Gate. /meanest-editor roasts the pitch like a veteran PR director. It gets up to 2 revisions. Under 7/10, I never see it.

The Fact Gate. /fact-check verifies every claim. Anything unverified goes under "Needs from you," not into the pitch.

The Human Gate. The bot never emails, DMs, submits, or creates a mailbox draft. I send everything.

Hard caps on top: 3 pitches a day, 5 reactive replies a week, one reporter per outlet per story.

If nothing clears the gates, I get no message. Silence is a feature.

One platform rule: Qwoted bans AI-written answers. My bot flags Qwoted requests, and I write those myself.

How to build AI skills that actually work:

Start by looking at everything you do in a given week by brain dumping all the stuff you hate doing into Claude.

Then run the Skill Test to determine which tasks should be turned into skills:

-takes 15+ minutes
-follows the same steps every time
-has a clear "good" output

Then run AOA:

1) Audit: make a list of the steps required to do the task today. Every step followed and every tool used.

2) DON'T SKIP THIS STEP: Optimize. Ask "does this step need to happen at all?" This is where you delete/simplify/standardize.

3) Automate what's left. Great skills have one job only.

Shortcut for the Audit step: Claude Cowork and Codex can now record you doing the task once and even draft the skill for you.

In Claude, this is called Record a Skill. In Codex it's called Record & Replay.

Every skill file needs 4 parts:

-a description in the words you actually say (this is the trigger)
-the steps you follow, in order
-a "never" list (the guardrails)
-5-10 real examples of "good"

A skill alone gets you 60-70% of the way there. The examples get you to 80-90%+.

I like to test my skills on 3 real examples. Then I'll iterate on the skill by fixing one issue at a time until it's near perfect.

When I did this for one of my clients we turned their onboarding workflow from 24 manual steps into 5 skills. 22 of 24 steps are now automated (2 of them stay human on purpose).

The Audit and Optimize steps are 80% of the work, the Automate step is the easy (and fun) part.

A simple framework I use to delegate tasks to AI agents is Why/Done/Access.

On your to do list app of choice try including these 3 lines in the description of each task:

Why:
Done:
Access:

Here's a few examples:

Send invoice to new client

-Why: get paid before month end
-Done: invoice sent, due date in the CRM
-Access: Stripe, signed proposal in Drive

Lock recording date with podcast guest

-Why: episode needs to ship this month
-Done: date on calendar, recording link sent
-Access: Gmail thread, calendar

This allows me to point any agent at my to do list and ask it to execute, and it has all the context needed without getting stuck. 

This is the prompt I give my agent every morning:

"Pull every task due today. Analyze the Why/Done/Access fields to get the context you need to fully complete each task. For any tasks that you’re unable to complete, do as much of the work as you possibly can then tee up the remaining work for me or my assistant to finish off.”

Make sure each of your descriptions pass this test: could someone who has never met you finish the task from it alone?

Yes, it's a pain for tasks like "book haircut."

But taking 30 seconds to add context is the boring work required to empower agents to fully execute tasks.

I spent 48 hours in Nashville with 25 elite startup founders.

My top 7 takeaways:

1. One guy went from $1,000 in revenue in June to $57K in August by optimizing his website for AI search. Use Claude Code/Codex to audit your site, rebuild it and fully optimize it for AI search.

2. Do permissionless projects. Some people in the room landed deals/meetings/opportunities so far out of their league by adding massive value with zero expectation of return.

3. 99.9% of peoples’ lives would be changed if they answered the question “how do I get 1,000 people to pay me $500 per year?”

4. Turn your capabilities into products. There are things that feel effortless to you that other people would pay a premium for. Productize them.

5. It’s far too easy to get shiny object syndrome in the age of AI. If your stack works, keep it. If a new tool doesn’t make you more money, save you time, or improve the quality of your product, drop it.

6. Context management is extremely important for avoiding agent lock in. Create an effective system for capturing context, storing it in a central knowledge base any agent can access, then build workflows that agents use to execute on that knowledge.

7. Everyone has 1 to 3 tasks that make them $10K per hour (or more). Figure out what those tasks are then focus all your effort on delegating or eliminating everything else on your plate.

It’s so energizing being around other founders especially since we spend most of our days huddled up behind a screen talking to Claude all day!

4 more interesting takeaways:

1. Sell before you build. There’s nothing worse than spending time/money building something nobody wants. Get someone to pay you first, then figure out how to deliver.

2. This group is ahead of 99.9% of people in terms of AI knowledge and a few of them had zero experience building skills. I’ve said it before and I’ll keep saying it, if you know how to build skills with AI (automated workflows), you’re in the top 0.1%.

3. Multiple different industries were represented at this event (HR, finance, tech, services, retail, etc.) but most everyone struggles with the same few problems, mainly distribution, funnel architecture, and consistent deal flow.

4. The folks in the room who were farthest ahead owned their distribution. That could be a huge IG audience, engaged email list, consistent website traffic, or something else entirely. But the common denominator between the most advanced people was a consistent stream of interested eyeballs.

If you want to get clients, make connections, build trust, etc...

You NEED to be hosting in person events.

This is my 4th month in a row hosting a local in-person AI For Business meetup in my city (Charlotte, NC).

I've made great friends, built valuable connections, and established myself as a local AI thought leader in 4 short months.

These are the exact steps I took to launch my meetup, and I highly encourage you to copy my process in your city/town:

1. Define your target audience. Mine is non-technical business owners. There are lots of meetups for devs, none for non-technical folks.

2. Pick a name for your meetup. I called mine AI For Business so people know exactly what they're getting by hearing the name. Don't overthink it.

3. Book a location to host the meetup. I rented a room at a local coworking space.

4. Create a registration page on Luma or Meetup. Make it clear what someone will take away from attending. Be specific.

5. Market your event in local business owner Facebook groups and by DMing people on LinkedIn/texting people direct invites.

6. Prepare a brief demo/presentation. At my first one I shared an Excalidraw diagram explaining what Skills are and how to build them. At this month's event we built a Brand Voice skill live on my computer. Again, don't overcomplicate this step.

7. Follow up with everyone who attended, ask what they liked/disliked then incorporate that feedback into the next one.

A few additional tips:

-Your first event may flop. It's ok, this is a long game. Keep doing them once a month and it'll grow.

-Find a well-connected person to co-host the event with you. The first one I ever did I co-hosted with a realtor. She invited all her friends/clients.

-Most people know nothing about AI. When you prepare your presentation, dumb it down then dumb it down again. Keep things SIMPLE.

Hopefully this helps you get your own local AI event/meetup off the ground. It has been a very fulfilling venture for me and my plan is to grow it exponentially and keep running it for years to come.

The Grok Bot setter we run on our free community (works for any business with inbound leads):

The trigger:

-Someone new comes in (free community, email list, etc)
-Bot sends them a DM written in our actual typing style, imperfections included
-One message, one free offer

The offer:

-Something personalized they get by filling out a short form
-Ours is a custom scaling plan. Yours could be an audit, a quote, a teardown, etc.
-We add 2 specific questions to the form: "want it by text?" and "interested in working with us?"

The reply loop:

-The bot checks for replies every hour
-It categorizes each reply and drafts a response into a Notion queue
-Every draft gets a status: Pending, Approved, or Revised
-Simple replies ("thanks", "send it over") get auto-approved
-Anything marked Revised, the bot studies what we changed and updates its own rules

The follow-up:

-No reply gets a follow up at 3 days, 7 days, and 1 month
-They reply: they exit follow-up and go back into the reply loop

The weekly dashboard:

-DMs sent
-Replies
-Response rate
-Free offers requested
-Free offers delivered
-Conversion to paid after DM
-Conversion to paid after free offer

The hourly reply checker burns through Grok But usage quickly so we're having our Dot do this part of the process since it's usage isn't currently charged.
